title: The Adjugate Behind Cramer's Rule and Cayley–Hamilton
description: The parent chain (cramers-rule) develops Cramer's rule via the adjugate. This entry answers its OQ-04-OQ-01: formalize the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton proof via the adjugate-reflexive identity adj(xI−A)·(xI−A) = χ_A(x)·I. Both Cramer's rule and Cayley–Hamilton rest on the same identity adj(B)·B = (det B)·I — Cramer applies it to a scalar matrix, Cayley–Hamilton to the characteristic matrix xI−A over R[X]. We package the adjugate identities, Cayley–Hamilton, minpoly ∣ charpoly, and the determinant form of Cramer's rule A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b, with 0 axioms.

mainTheorems.name: adjugate_charmatrix_mul
mainTheorems.description: The adjugate-reflexive identity and the algebraic heart of Cayley–Hamilton: over R[X], the adjugate of the characteristic matrix xI − A times the characteristic matrix equals the characteristic polynomial times the identity, adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I. Instantiates Mathlib's general adjugate_mul at B = charmatrix M.
mainTheorems.leanType: (M : Matrix n n R) → adjugate (charmatrix M) * charmatrix M = M.charpoly • 1

mainTheorems.name: cayley_hamilton
mainTheorems.description: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem: every matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial, χ_A(A) = 0. Obtained from the adjugate-reflexive identity by passing to Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluating at A (Mathlib: aeval_self_charpoly).
mainTheorems.leanType: (M : Matrix n n R) → aeval M M.charpoly = 0

mainTheorems.name: adjugate_mulVec_solve
mainTheorems.description: The determinant form of Cramer's rule: the adjugate solves A x = b up to the determinant, A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b. When det A is a unit this yields the explicit solution x = (det A)⁻¹ · adj A · b. Rests on the same adjugate identity A·adj A = (det A)·I that drives Cayley–Hamilton.
mainTheorems.leanType: (A : Matrix n n R) → (b : n → R) → A *ᵥ (adjugate A *ᵥ b) = A.det • b

mainTheorems.name: mul_adjugate_eq
mainTheorems.description: The scalar adjugate identity A·adj(A) = (det A)·I — the common source of both Cramer's rule (B = A) and Cayley–Hamilton (B = xI − A). Instantiates Mathlib's mul_adjugate.
mainTheorems.leanType: (A : Matrix n n R) → A * adjugate A = A.det • 1

mainTheorems.name: minpoly_dvd_charpoly
mainTheorems.description: Over a field, the minimal polynomial of A divides its characteristic polynomial — a direct consequence of Cayley–Hamilton (χ_A annihilates A, so minpoly ∣ χ_A).
mainTheorems.leanType: {K : Type*} → [Field K] → (M : Matrix n n K) → minpoly K M ∣ M.charpoly

overview.historicalContext:
The adjugate (classical adjoint) of a square matrix A is the transpose of its cofactor matrix, and it satisfies the fundamental identity adj(A)·A = A·adj(A) = (det A)·I. This single identity underlies two cornerstones of linear algebra. **Cramer's rule** applies it to A itself: when det A is invertible, A⁻¹ = (det A)⁻¹·adj(A), so the system Ax = b has the explicit solution x = (det A)⁻¹·adj(A)·b. The **Cayley–Hamilton theorem** applies it to the characteristic matrix B = xI − A over the polynomial ring R[X]: since det(xI − A) = χ_A(x), the identity reads adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I, and passing to Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluating at A telescopes the right factor to zero, yielding χ_A(A) = 0.

Mathlib formalizes the adjugate identity (adjugate_mul, mul_adjugate) and proves Cayley–Hamilton exactly via this route (aeval_self_charpoly, whose proof opens with adjugate (charmatrix M) * charmatrix M = M.charpoly • 1). This entry answers the parent's OQ-04-OQ-01 by exposing the adjugate-reflexive identity as a named lemma, restating Cayley–Hamilton and its minpoly consequence, and recording the determinant form of Cramer's rule — making explicit that both theorems flow from the same adjugate identity.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton theorem via the adjugate-reflexive identity adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I, and tie it to Cramer's rule through their shared adjugate identity adj(B)·B = (det B)·I. Record Cayley–Hamilton, minpoly ∣ charpoly, and the determinant form of Cramer's rule.
overview.proofStrategy: adjugate_charmatrix_mul is adjugate_mul applied to the characteristic matrix charmatrix M, using that charpoly M is by definition det(charmatrix M). cayley_hamilton restates Mathlib's aeval_self_charpoly (proved by lifting the adjugate identity to Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluating at A). minpoly_dvd_charpoly is Mathlib's lemma. adjugate_mulVec_solve rewrites A·(adj A · b) via mulVec associativity to (A·adj A)·b = (det A · I)·b = det A · b, using mul_adjugate, smul_mulVec_assoc, one_mulVec.
keyInsights: One identity, two theorems: adj(B)·B = (det B)·I gives Cramer's rule when B = A (scalar entries) and Cayley–Hamilton when B = xI − A (polynomial entries).

Cayley–Hamilton is NOT obtained by naively substituting x = A into χ_A(x)·I = adj(xI−A)·(xI−A): the coefficient ring Matrix n n R is non-commutative, so one must work in Polynomial (Matrix n n R) and evaluate, where the right factor (xI − A) telescopes to zero.
The determinant form of Cramer's rule A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b is the adjugate identity applied to a vector; dividing by det A (when invertible) gives the classical explicit solution.
Over a field, Cayley–Hamilton immediately yields minpoly A ∣ charpoly A, bounding the degree of the minimal polynomial by n.
Exhibiting the shared adjugate source clarifies why determinants, inverses (Cramer), and the characteristic polynomial (Cayley–Hamilton) are facets of one cofactor identity.

sections.title: Overview: One Adjugate Identity Behind Two Theorems
sections.summary: Imports and module docstring. States the parent chain's open question (formalize the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton proof via the adjugate-reflexive property adj(xI−A)·(xI−A) = χ_A(x)·I) and the unifying observation: both Cramer's rule and Cayley–Hamilton are instances of the single adjugate identity adjugate B · B = (det B)·I — Cramer's rule with the scalar matrix B = A, Cayley–Hamilton with the characteristic matrix B = xI−A over R[X], where det(xI−A) = χ_A(x). Lists the main results and sets up a commutative ring R with a finite index type n.
sections.mathContext: Common source: $\operatorname{adj}(B)\,B = (\det B)\,I$. Cramer: $B = A$. Cayley–Hamilton: $B = xI - A$, $\det(xI-A) = \chi_A(x)$, then evaluate at $A$.

sections.title: Section III: The Second Adjugate Identity A·adj(A) = (det A)·I
sections.summary: mul_adjugate_eq records the companion form of the universal identity, A·adjugate A = (det A)·I (Mathlib's mul_adjugate). Where Section I used adj(B)·B on the characteristic matrix, this is the same cofactor identity on the scalar matrix A — the source from which Cramer's rule flows.
sections.mathContext: $A\,\mathrm{adj}(A) = (\det A)\,I$, the scalar-matrix face of $\mathrm{adj}(B)B=(\det B)I$.

sections.title: Section IV: Cramer's Rule as the Adjugate Applied to a Vector
sections.summary: adjugate_mulVec_solve applies the second identity to a vector: A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b, via mulVec_mulVec associativity, mul_adjugate, smul_mulVec_assoc, and one_mulVec. When det A is a unit, dividing gives the classical Cramer solution x = (det A)⁻¹·adj A·b — exhibiting Cramer's rule and Cayley–Hamilton as two specializations of one identity.
sections.mathContext: $A\,(\mathrm{adj}(A)\,b) = (\det A)\,b$; $\det A$ a unit $\Rightarrow x = (\det A)^{-1}\mathrm{adj}(A)\,b$.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 71 lines and 5 theorems exhibiting the adjugate identity adj(B)·B = (det B)·I as the common source of Cramer's rule and the Cayley–Hamilton theorem. It states the adjugate-reflexive identity adj(xI − A)·(xI − A) = χ_A(x)·I, Cayley–Hamilton χ_A(A) = 0, minpoly ∣ charpoly, and the determinant form of Cramer's rule A·(adj A · b) = (det A)·b.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's OQ-04-OQ-01 by formalizing the algebraic Cayley–Hamilton proof through the adjugate-reflexive identity, and makes explicit that Cramer's rule and Cayley–Hamilton are two applications of one cofactor identity — Cramer for scalar matrices, Cayley–Hamilton for the characteristic matrix over R[X]. The adjugate-solution lemma is a reusable bridge between the adjugate and linear-system solving.
